module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Combinatorial representation of the recurrence $a(n+2) = 2a(n+1) + 2a(n)$

A028859 (OEIS): $a(n+2) = 2 \cdot a(n+1) + 2 \cdot a(n)$; $a(0) = 1$, $a(1) = 3$.

*References:*
- [A028859](https://oeis.org/A028859)
- [arxiv/2605.22763](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763) *Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search* by George Tsoukalas et al.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace OeisA28859


/--
A028859 (OEIS): $a(n+2) = 2 \cdot a(n+1) + 2 \cdot a(n)$; $a(0) = 1$, $a(1) = 3$.
-/
def a (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  match n with
  | 0 => 1
  | 1 => 3
  | (n + 2) => 2 * a (n + 1) + 2 * a n
termination_by n

set_option linter.unusedVariables false


@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_0 : a 0 = 1 := by native_decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_1 : a 1 = 3 := by native_decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_2 : a 2 = 8 := by native_decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_3 : a 3 = 22 := by native_decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_4 : a 4 = 60 := by native_decide


/--
Conjecture: The sequence a(n) is also the number of compositions of $n$ into positive integers
such that adjacent parts and the largest part differ by at most 1. - _Gus Wiseman_, May 19 2020

A formal proof has been found with the methods described in
[arxiv/2605.22763](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763).
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
"https://github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures/blob/a32396489dcb8f86c3549b93aa358ac6a10a3a1f/FormalConjectures/OEIS/28859.wip.lean#L402"]
theorem exists_finset_sequence (n : ℕ) :
    let L := n + 1
    let Sequence := Fin L → ℕ
    let S : Set Sequence :=
      {σ : Sequence |
        L > 0 ∧
          (∀ i : Fin L, σ i > 0) ∧
            let max_val := Finset.sup Finset.univ σ
            (∀ k : ℕ, 1 ≤ k ∧ k ≤ max_val → ∃ i : Fin L, σ i = k) ∧
            (∀ i j : Fin L, i < j → j.val ≠ i.val + 1 → σ i ≥ σ j)}
    ∃ (F : Finset Sequence), (F : Set Sequence) = S ∧ F.card = a n := by
    sorry

end OeisA28859

findings.description: The docstring at lines 65–66 describes compositions of n whose adjacent parts and largest part differ by at most 1. Neither the cited conjecture nor the Lean statement says this. The Lean correctly counts length-(n+1) sequences whose values form an initial interval of positive integers and whose non-adjacent parts are weakly decreasing. Only the documentation is wrong; the formal statement is faithful.
findings.source_evidence: OEIS A028859, Gus Wiseman's May 19, 2020 comment: “Conjecture: Also the number of length n + 1 sequences that cover an initial interval of positive integers and whose non-adjacent parts are weakly decreasing.” The comment separately directs the composition-counting version to A333148. Read at https://oeis.org/A028859/internal through its text mirror.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the first paragraph of the theorem docstring with: “Wiseman's conjecture: a(n) is the number of length n+1 sequences of positive integers whose values form an initial interval and whose non-adjacent parts are weakly decreasing. — Gus Wiseman, May 19 2020.” Leave the Lean statement unchanged.

sources_consulted: https://arxiv.org/e-print/2605.22763 (v2 LaTeX source, particularly the OEIS evaluation section)
review.notes: All seven declarations were checked. No mathematical misformalization was found. In /workspace/review/scratch.lean, I proved the set predicate equivalent to the source description, proved that every value is at most the sequence length, and verified satisfiability for every n. Enumeration for lengths 1–6 gives 1, 3, 8, 22, 60, 164; the recurrence and all five test lemmas agree with OEIS. The solved status is supported by OEIS's June 2026 proof comments. The separately published AlphaProof Nexus proof was checked after toolchain-compatibility edits in /workspace/review/external_proof_check.lean; a transport to the exact reviewed statement depends only on propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound. All review edits were confined to /workspace/review/.
